title: Physics Laboratory Technology
source_note: Grounded in standard NUC-aligned physics laboratory technology curricula: measurement and error analysis, mechanics, heat, optics, and electricity practicals typical of a 200-level Science Laboratory Technology programme.

questions.question: A vernier caliper has a main scale reading of 2.30 cm and a vernier scale that coincides at the 4th division, with a least count of 0.01 cm. What is the total reading?
questions.explanation: The total reading is the main scale reading plus (vernier coincidence x least count): 2.30 + (4 x 0.01) = 2.34 cm.

questions.question: What is the least count of a standard micrometer screw gauge with a pitch of 0.5 mm and 50 divisions on the circular scale?
options: 0.1 mm
questions.explanation: Least count = pitch / number of divisions on circular scale = 0.5 mm / 50 = 0.01 mm.

questions.question: Zero error in a micrometer screw gauge occurs when:
options: The zero of the circular scale does not coincide with the reference line when the jaws are closed
The instrument has been dropped
The pitch is incorrectly manufactured
The object being measured is too small
questions.correct_answer: The zero of the circular scale does not coincide with the reference line when the jaws are closed
questions.explanation: Zero error is a systematic error where the closed-jaw reading is not exactly zero, requiring a correction to be applied to all readings.

questions.question: In the equation for the simple pendulum, T = 2π√(l/g), what does the term 'l' represent in a lab experiment?
options: The effective length from the point of suspension to the centre of the bob
The diameter of the bob
The length of the retort stand
The amplitude of oscillation
questions.correct_answer: The effective length from the point of suspension to the centre of the bob
questions.explanation: The effective length is measured from the fixed support to the centre of mass of the bob, as this is the radius of the circular arc the bob traces.

questions.question: A student times 20 oscillations of a simple pendulum and records 40.0 s. What is the period of one oscillation?
questions.explanation: Period T = total time / number of oscillations = 40.0 s / 20 = 2.0 s.

questions.question: Why is it standard practice to time multiple oscillations rather than a single oscillation when determining the period of a pendulum?
options: To reduce the percentage error caused by human reaction time in starting/stopping the stopwatch
Because a single oscillation cannot be observed
To make the pendulum swing faster
Because the pendulum bob changes mass over time
questions.correct_answer: To reduce the percentage error caused by human reaction time in starting/stopping the stopwatch
questions.explanation: Averaging over many oscillations spreads the fixed timing (reaction) error over a longer interval, reducing its relative contribution to the measured period.

questions.question: In a Hooke's law experiment, a spring extends by 4.0 cm when a load of 2.0 N is applied. What is the spring constant k?
options: 50 N/m
8 N/m
questions.correct_answer: 50 N/m

questions.question: In the Hooke's law experiment, why must the applied load remain within the elastic limit of the spring?
options: Beyond the elastic limit the spring is permanently deformed and no longer obeys F = kx
Beyond the elastic limit the spring becomes heavier
It has no effect on the results
The spring changes colour beyond the elastic limit
questions.correct_answer: Beyond the elastic limit the spring is permanently deformed and no longer obeys F = kx
questions.explanation: Hooke's law only holds for elastic deformation; exceeding the elastic limit causes plastic deformation and non-linear, non-recoverable extension.

questions.question: Which apparatus is used to determine the density of an irregularly shaped solid that sinks in water?
options: A eureka (displacement) can and a measuring cylinder
A micrometer screw gauge only
A spring balance only
A thermometer
questions.correct_answer: A eureka (displacement) can and a measuring cylinder
questions.explanation: The volume of an irregular solid is found by measuring the volume of water it displaces, then density is mass divided by that volume.

questions.question: In calorimetry, the method of mixtures is based on which principle?
options: Heat lost by the hotter body equals heat gained by the colder body (assuming no heat loss to surroundings)
Heat always increases the volume of a liquid
Specific heat capacity is constant for all substances
Temperature is directly proportional to mass
questions.correct_answer: Heat lost by the hotter body equals heat gained by the colder body (assuming no heat loss to surroundings)
questions.explanation: The method of mixtures applies conservation of energy: in an insulated system, heat energy lost by the hot substance is gained by the cold substance and the calorimeter.

questions.question: A calorimeter of negligible heat capacity contains 100 g of water at 20°C. 50 g of metal at 100°C is added and the final temperature is 25°C. Using specific heat capacity of water = 4.2 J/g°C, what is the heat gained by the water?
What is the main purpose of stirring the water in a calorimeter during a specific heat capacity experiment?
options: To ensure a uniform temperature distribution throughout the liquid before taking readings
To cool the water rapidly
To increase the mass of water
To dissolve the calorimeter
questions.correct_answer: To ensure a uniform temperature distribution throughout the liquid before taking readings
questions.explanation: Stirring prevents localized hot or cold spots, so the thermometer reading reflects the true average temperature of the system.

questions.question: Why is a lagged (insulated) calorimeter preferred over a bare metal container in heat experiments?
options: It minimizes heat exchange with the surroundings, reducing experimental error
It makes the calorimeter lighter
It increases the specific heat capacity of the water
It is required for legal safety reasons only
questions.correct_answer: It minimizes heat exchange with the surroundings, reducing experimental error
questions.explanation: Lagging reduces heat loss/gain to the environment during the experiment, improving the accuracy of the measured heat energy transfer.

questions.question: In determining the refractive index of a glass block using the real-and-apparent depth method, what quantity is measured?
options: Real depth and apparent depth of an object viewed through the glass block
The mass and volume of the glass block
The angle of the glass block's edges only
The temperature of the glass block
questions.correct_answer: Real depth and apparent depth of an object viewed through the glass block
questions.explanation: Refractive index n = real depth / apparent depth, found by comparing the true thickness of the block to its apparent thickness when viewed from above.

questions.question: In the glass block refraction experiment using pins, why must the eye be positioned so that the two viewing pins appear to be in a straight line with the two pins on the other side of the block?
options: To ensure the line of sight accurately traces the path of the refracted ray
To prevent the pins from falling over
To measure the mass of the glass block
It has no bearing on accuracy
questions.correct_answer: To ensure the line of sight accurately traces the path of the refracted ray
questions.explanation: Collinearity of the pins as viewed by the eye confirms the observer is sighting exactly along the emergent ray, which is essential for accurately marking the ray path.

questions.question: Which formula is used to determine the focal length of a convex lens using the 'no-parallax' method with an illuminated object and a pin?
options: f = u x v
f = u + v
f = u/v
questions.explanation: The thin lens formula relates focal length f to object distance u and image distance v as 1/f = 1/v + 1/u for a real image.

questions.question: A convex lens forms a sharp image on a screen when the object is 30 cm away and the image distance is 15 cm. What is the focal length of the lens?
options: 10 cm
45 cm
15 cm
questions.correct_answer: 10 cm

questions.question: In a spectrometer experiment to determine the refractive index of a prism material, which two angles must be measured?
options: The angle of the prism and the angle of minimum deviation
The angle of incidence and the height of the prism
Only the angle of the prism
The angle between the two lenses of the spectrometer
questions.correct_answer: The angle of the prism and the angle of minimum deviation
questions.explanation: Refractive index is calculated from n = sin[(A+D)/2] / sin(A/2), where A is the prism angle and D is the angle of minimum deviation.

questions.question: Before taking readings, a spectrometer must be adjusted so that the telescope and collimator are both set to receive:
options: Parallel rays
Converging rays
Diverging rays
Polarized rays
questions.correct_answer: Parallel rays
questions.explanation: The collimator produces a parallel beam from the slit, and the telescope must be focused for parallel rays so both are correctly adjusted for infinity.

questions.question: In a resistivity/Ohm's law experiment, what is the purpose of a rheostat connected in the circuit?
options: To vary the current flowing through the circuit for a range of readings
To measure the voltage directly
To permanently fix the current at one value
To store electrical charge
questions.correct_answer: To vary the current flowing through the circuit for a range of readings
questions.explanation: A rheostat is a variable resistor used to adjust current, allowing the student to obtain multiple voltage-current data points for plotting a graph.

questions.question: In a Wheatstone bridge experiment, the bridge is said to be balanced when:
options: No current flows through the galvanometer
The current through the galvanometer is at its maximum
All four resistors have equal resistance
The battery is fully discharged
questions.correct_answer: No current flows through the galvanometer
questions.explanation: At balance, the potential at the junction between the two arms is equal on both sides, so no current flows through the galvanometer bridging them.

questions.question: In a metre bridge (a practical form of the Wheatstone bridge) experiment, the balance point is found at 40 cm from one end with a known resistance of 6 Ω in that gap. What is the unknown resistance?
options: 9 Ω
4 Ω
questions.correct_answer: 9 Ω
questions.explanation: Using R_unknown/R_known = (100-l)/l = 60/40, R_unknown = 6 x 60/40 = 9 Ω.

questions.question: What is the primary function of a potentiometer in determining the EMF of a cell?
options: To compare an unknown EMF against a known EMF using a null (zero-current) deflection method
To directly convert EMF into heat
To amplify the EMF of the cell
To measure the mass of the cell
questions.correct_answer: To compare an unknown EMF against a known EMF using a null (zero-current) deflection method
questions.explanation: A potentiometer measures EMF without drawing current from the cell at the balance point, giving a more accurate measurement than a voltmeter, which draws some current.

questions.question: An analogue multimeter set to measure DC voltage must be connected in the circuit:
options: In parallel with the component
In series with the component
Directly across the battery terminals only
In series with the ammeter
questions.correct_answer: In parallel with the component
questions.explanation: A voltmeter (or multimeter set to voltage mode) has high internal resistance and is connected in parallel so it measures potential difference without significantly altering circuit current.

questions.question: An ammeter must be connected in a circuit:
options: In series with the component
In parallel with the component
Directly across the cell only
Never connected to a closed circuit
questions.correct_answer: In series with the component
questions.explanation: An ammeter has very low internal resistance and is placed in series so the full circuit current flows through it for accurate measurement.

questions.question: Which of the following is a systematic error, as opposed to a random error?
options: A zero error in a measuring instrument that is not corrected for
Slight variation in reaction time when using a stopwatch
Parallax error that varies from reading to reading
Fluctuation in room temperature during readings
questions.correct_answer: A zero error in a measuring instrument that is not corrected for
questions.explanation: Systematic errors consistently bias every reading in the same direction (e.g. an uncorrected zero error), unlike random errors which vary unpredictably.

questions.question: What safety precaution is essential when handling a mercury-in-glass thermometer in the physics laboratory?
options: Avoid dropping or breaking it, and report any breakage immediately due to mercury toxicity
Store it upside down at all times
Heat it rapidly to check calibration
Use it to stir chemical solutions
questions.correct_answer: Avoid dropping or breaking it, and report any breakage immediately due to mercury toxicity
questions.explanation: Mercury is toxic and volatile; breakage requires careful containment and reporting to avoid exposure, so lab technicians must handle these thermometers with care.

questions.question: When using a travelling microscope to measure small lengths, why should parallax error be checked before taking readings?
options: Because misalignment between the crosswire and the object can cause a reading error that varies with the observer's eye position
Because it affects the colour of the object
Because it changes the object's actual size
Because the microscope cannot function without it
questions.correct_answer: Because misalignment between the crosswire and the object can cause a reading error that varies with the observer's eye position
questions.explanation: Parallax occurs when the line of sight is not perpendicular to the scale, causing apparent shifts in reading; eliminating it ensures accurate length measurement.

questions.question: In a simple electrical experiment measuring resistance, why should the current be kept low and switched off between readings?
options: To prevent excessive heating of the resistor, which would change its resistance value
To make the ammeter needle move faster
To increase the EMF of the battery
Because low current damages the rheostat
questions.correct_answer: To prevent excessive heating of the resistor, which would change its resistance value
questions.explanation: Resistance can vary with temperature; keeping current low and switching off between readings minimizes self-heating (Joule heating) that would distort results.

questions.question: In an experiment to verify Boyle's law using a Bourdon gauge apparatus, what two quantities are recorded at constant temperature?
options: Pressure and volume of the trapped air column
Temperature and time
Mass and length of the tube
Current and voltage
questions.correct_answer: Pressure and volume of the trapped air column
questions.explanation: Boyle's law experiments record pressure readings from the gauge against the corresponding volume (length) of trapped gas at constant temperature to show PV = constant.

questions.question: What is the correct procedure for reading a scale to avoid parallax error when using a metre rule and a pointer?
options: Position the eye directly perpendicular to the scale at the level of the pointer
Read the scale from an angle above the pointer
Read the scale as quickly as possible from any angle
Always read from the left side of the rule
questions.correct_answer: Position the eye directly perpendicular to the scale at the level of the pointer
questions.explanation: Viewing perpendicular to the scale (line of sight normal to the ruler) at the pointer's level eliminates the apparent shift caused by parallax.

questions.question: A student records five readings for the period of a pendulum: 2.01 s, 2.05 s, 1.98 s, 2.02 s, 2.04 s. What best describes the type of error causing this spread?
options: Random error
Systematic error
Gross error only
Instrumental zero error
questions.correct_answer: Random error
questions.explanation: The small, unpredictable variation around a central value in repeated measurements is characteristic of random error, often reduced by averaging.

questions.question: Why should electrical circuits in the laboratory be checked by a demonstrator before switching on the power supply?
options: To verify correct wiring and prevent short circuits or damage to components and injury to the student
To make the experiment take longer
Because it is required only for AC circuits
To reduce the resistance of the circuit
questions.correct_answer: To verify correct wiring and prevent short circuits or damage to components and injury to the student
questions.explanation: Pre-checking wiring prevents short circuits, reversed polarity, or overloaded components, protecting both equipment and the student from electrical hazards.

questions.question: What is the correct SI unit for measuring the extension of a spring in a Hooke's law experiment for use directly in F = kx (with k in N/m)?
options: Metre (m)
Centimetre (cm)
Millimetre (mm)
Kilometre (km)
questions.correct_answer: Metre (m)
questions.explanation: For the spring constant k to come out in the SI unit N/m, extension x must be converted to metres before substituting into F = kx.
